source: Each branch has the same voltage, 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ⋯, and adding a branch lowers R_eq.
Students think adding a resistor in parallel raises the total resistance.
In parallel, each resistor gets its own path between the same two points. That changes everything you just learned about series circuits: now the voltage is shared and the currents add.

Each branch connects directly across the same two points, so each has the same voltage $V$. Each branch's current is $V/R_i$, and at the junction the currents add: $I = \dfrac{V}{R_1} + \dfrac{V}{R_2} + \cdots$. If one resistor $R_{\text{eq}}$ is to draw the same $I$, then $\dfrac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \cdots$. Every extra branch is an extra path, so the total current goes up and $R_{\text{eq}}$ goes down, below even the smallest resistor.

Parallel: same voltage across each branch; the branch currents add; $\dfrac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \cdots$. For two: $R_{\text{eq}} = \dfrac{R_1R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$. For $n$ equal resistors: $R/n$.
Three bulbs in parallel: each gets the full battery voltage. Try it in the Circuit Builder.
A $6\,\Omega$ and a $3\,\Omega$ resistor are in parallel on a $12\,\text{V}$ battery. Find the branch currents, the total current and $R_{\text{eq}}$.

Thinking that adding a resistor in parallel raises the total resistance, because there is “more resistance” in the circuit. A new branch is a new path, so more current flows from the same battery, and that means less total resistance. Check: $R_{\text{eq}}$ of a parallel group is always smaller than its smallest branch.
A voltmeter measures the voltage between two points, so it goes in parallel across the part it measures. A good voltmeter has a very large resistance, so almost no current is diverted through it.
The outlets in a house are wired in parallel, so every appliance gets the full voltage and works whether or not the others are on.
